subsystems.name: Neural culture
subsystems.role: the living processor: a few hundred thousand neurons that grow into a spontaneously active network.
parts: cortical neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (or rodent primary cells)
adhesion coating such as poly-D-lysine and laminin

subsystems.name: Electrode interface
subsystems.role: the two-way plug between wet tissue and dry electronics.
parts: microelectrode array (often 60 electrodes at roughly 100–200 µm spacing)
high-density CMOS array with tens of thousands of electrodes at 10–20 µm spacing

subsystems.name: Life support
subsystems.role: keeps tissue at body conditions for weeks to months, not hours.
parts: bubble traps and sterile fluid lines

subsystems.name: Readout electronics
subsystems.role: detects the millivolt spikes of individual neurons and turns them into data.

subsystems.name: Stimulation path
subsystems.role: writes signals back into the network — the basis of any learning.
parts: optogenetic light source and genetically encoded ion channels, where used

subsystems.name: Closed-loop controller and body
subsystems.role: decodes network activity into action and encodes the robot's senses back as stimulation.
parts: real-time computer running a decoding model
encoder mapping sensor readings to stimulation patterns

buildSteps.title: Derive and quality-check neurons
buildSteps.detail: Skin or blood cells are reprogrammed to stem cells, then driven to become cortical neurons over several weeks and screened for healthy spontaneous firing.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the chip
buildSteps.detail: A CMOS or glass substrate is patterned with metal electrodes, insulated except at the tips, and coated with adhesion proteins that let neurons grip it.

buildSteps.title: Seed and mature the culture
buildSteps.detail: Cells are plated at a few thousand per square millimetre, fed every few days, and left for two to four weeks until the network settles into stable, patterned activity.

buildSteps.title: Close the electrical loop
buildSteps.detail: The array is wired to amplifiers and a computer that can record spikes and deliver stimulation within a few milliseconds — fast enough for the loop to feel instantaneous to the cells.

buildSteps.title: Train the network
buildSteps.detail: Stimulation patterns are paired with feedback chosen to exploit spike-timing-dependent plasticity, so the network's firing slowly reorganises toward the task rather than drifting randomly.

buildSteps.title: Connect a body
buildSteps.detail: Decoded output drives robot joints or a virtual agent's controls; the robot's sensors are re-encoded as stimulation, so the culture acts on the world it is being told about.

buildSteps.title: Engineer field life support
buildSteps.detail: For anything beyond a bench, the incubator becomes a miniaturised, shock-tolerant perfusion system with sterile fluidics, temperature control and waste removal — the hardest step, since a robot that falls over must not kill its own brain.

buildSteps.title: Build in redundancy
buildSteps.detail: Cultures die, so a practical machine would carry several independent units, automatic health monitoring and the ability to switch control when one degrades.

prerequisites.why: without a steady supply of healthy, uniform neural tissue there is no reliable device.
laboratory CMOS arrays can stimulate and record thousands of sites, but not yet for months at a time in a moving machine.
the loop must close in milliseconds, which needs dedicated hardware rather than recorded-and-analysed-later data.
cultures do show plasticity, but the stable, generalisable learning needed for useful tasks is not demonstrated.

prerequisites.tech: Long-term life support outside an incubator
prerequisites.why: there is no established way to keep cortical tissue viable for years in a portable, powered, moving platform.
rules for devices containing human-derived neural tissue, and for when they should be switched off, do not yet exist.

pathway.milestone: cultured networks on multi-electrode arrays displaying stimulus-dependent activity; in 2022 human and mouse neurons in a dish were reported to learn a simple paddle game within minutes
pathway.unlocks: proof that living networks can be trained through an electrode interface at all.

pathway.milestone: closed-loop laboratory hybrids where a neural culture controls a simple robot or simulated body and improves with practice
pathway.unlocks: benchmark tasks and the first honest comparison against conventional spiking hardware on energy per decision.

pathway.milestone: neural cultures used as low-power accelerators for narrow pattern-recognition problems, accessed remotely as a service
pathway.unlocks: a commercial reason to fund the life-support engineering.

pathway.milestone: portable, self-maintaining neural units with reliable fluidics and months-long viability
pathway.unlocks: hybrid machines that leave the lab.

pathway.milestone: directed neuron-to-tissue interfaces for prosthetics, where cultured or grafted neurons talk to a patient's nervous system
pathway.unlocks: prosthetic control that borrows biology's own signalling — far more plausible near-term than fully biological robots doing general labour.
